audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed final stress; phonological words are stressed monosyllables or iambic sesquisyllables with unstressed presyllables) rests on the standard modern reference grammar (Alves 2006, Pacific Linguistics 580), which I fetched sources from the ANU open repository and in which both quoted sentences appear verbatim (pp. 16 and 19). The earlier SIL phonology article (Watson 1964, MKS 1, p.144), fetched sources and scanned now, independently describes words as a main syllable optionally preceded by an unstressed presyllable. No instrumental stress study of Pacoh was found; the only fuller work is Alves's own 2000 dissertation, superseded by the 2006 book. Only housekeeping needed: register the now-held file and correct the locator to pp. 16, 19 (PDF 28, 31) instead of 'pp. 16, 21-24 (PDF 27-30)'.

sources.citation: Alves 2006, A grammar of Pacoh (Pacific Linguistics 580), PDF from ANU Open Research Repository, pp. 16, 21-24 (PDF pages 27-30), read 2026-08-31
sources.quote: Every phonological word has a single stress on final syllables. [...] there are only two types of phonological words in Pacoh: stressed monosyllabic and ultimate-stressed bisyllabic words.

sources.citation: Alves, Mark J. 2006. A grammar of Pacoh: a Mon-Khmer language of the central highlands of Vietnam. Pacific Linguistics 580. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU. xii+129 pp. (ANU Open Research Repository, hdl 1885/146283)
sources.quote: p.16: 'Every phonological word has a single stress on final syllables.' p.17: 'Pacoh presyllables ... These syllables are never stressed and have only one mora.' p.19: 'The phonological word in Pacoh, having at most two syllables, always has one main stress, which is always final. Thus, there are only two types of phonological words in Pacoh: stressed monosyllabic and ultimate-stressed bisyllabic words. Stressed syllables are pronounced longer and with higher loudness.'

sources.citation: Watson, Richard. 1964. Pacoh phonemes. Mon-Khmer Studies 1: 135-148. (sealang.net MKS archive; no text layer, scanned at 300 dpi)
sources.quote: 'Pacoh words are made up of a main syllable which may be preceded by an unstressed presyllable. Presyllables are often morphologically significant.' (only stress statement in the article; grep of scanned text finds no other occurrence of 'stress')
